JetFlow: Breaking the Scaling Ceiling of Speculative Decoding with Parallel Tree Drafting

Lanxiang Hu Affiliation: UC San Diego    Zhaoxiang Feng Affiliation: UC San Diego    Yulun Wu Affiliation:  Zhejiang University    Haoran Yuan Affiliation: UIUC    Yujie Zhao Affiliation: UC San Diego    Yu-Yang Qian Affiliation: Nanjing University    Bojun Wang Affiliation: StepFun    Daxin Jiang Affiliation: StepFun    Yibo Zhu Affiliation: StepFun    Tajana Rosing Affiliation: UC San Diego    Hao Zhang Affiliation: UC San Diego
Abstract

Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs) by drafting multiple tokens and verifying them in parallel, but it faces a scaling limitation: increasing the draft budget improves speed only when acceptance remains high and drafting overhead stays low. This ceiling has been difficult to break because prior head-based SD methods face a causality-efficiency dilemma. Autoregressive drafters produce path-conditioned candidates that are effective for tree speculative decoding with higher acceptance length, but their drafting cost grows with tree depth. Bidirectional block-diffusion drafters generate all positions in one pass, but their branch-agnostic marginals can form individually plausible yet mutually inconsistent trees, wasting budget and reducing acceptance. We propose JetFlow, a head-based SD framework that combines one-forward drafting efficiency with branch-wise causal conditioning. JetFlow trains a causal parallel draft head over fused hidden states from the frozen target model, producing candidate trees whose scores align with the target model’s autoregressive factorization. This enables JetFlow to convert larger draft budgets into longer accepted prefixes and higher end-to-end speedup. Across math, coding, and chat benchmarks on dense and MoE Qwen3 models, JetFlow consistently outperforms bidirectional-head and tree-based SD baselines. On H100 GPUs, JetFlow achieves up to 9.64×9.64\times speedup on MATH-500 and 4.58×4.58\times on open-ended conversational workloads, with further latency gains demonstrated through vLLM integration under realistic serving loads. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/hao-ai-lab/JetFlow.

1 Introduction

Modern autoregressive (AR) Large Language Models (LLMs) operate under a simple yet costly bottleneck: decoding remains largely serial. This sequential generation process makes latency a major challenge when they are deployed in applications such as math (Wei et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2025), coding (Deng and others, 2025; Jain et al., 2025) and other agentic reasoning tasks (Patil et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025), where models often perform long generations.

Existing approaches address this challenge by either incorporating multi-token prediction (MTP) during pre-training or mid-training (Gloeckle et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026), or post-training methods that adapt pretrained LLMs into diffusion LLMs (dLLMs) at the costs of varying degrees of performance degradation (Zhao et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025). In contrast, applying speculative decoding (SD) at inference time to reduce generation latency while preserving quality (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023).

Among these techniques, SD stands out for its low adaptation cost and simplicity. On one hand, prior work shows that SD performance can be substantially improved through lightweight draft-model alignment, oftentimes less than 1B training tokens (Liu et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024; Goel et al., 2024). On the other hand, head-based methods such as Medusa and EAGLE reduce deployment complexity by avoiding the conventional separate draft-target model setup (Cai et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b). More recent head-based methods such as EAGLE-3 (Li et al., 2025) and DFlash (Chen et al., 2026) continue to improve drafting quality and reducing drafting cost for better end-to-end acceleration. Despite these advances, head-based SD still faces a causality-efficiency dilemma. Autoregressive drafters such as EAGLE produce high-quality path-conditioned candidates but require sequential draft passes as tree depth grows. Bidirectional block-diffusion drafters such as DFlash produces drafts in one pass, but their branch-agnostic marginals can form individually plausible yet mutually inconsistent trees, wasting budget and reducing acceptance.

We propose JetFlow, a SD paradigm designed to break this causality–efficiency dilemma: JetFlow trains a causal parallel draft head to predict multiple tree nodes in one forward pass while preserving branch-wise causal conditioning through block-level causal attention over hidden states. This gives each branch a path-conditioned draft distribution aligned with the target model’s autoregressive factorization, enabling tree acceptance to better scale with additional draft budget.

Empirically, JetFlow demonstrates significant efficiency gains. In the low-token-budget regime with 16 draft tokens, JetFlow achieves competitive end-to-end speedup. In the high-token-budget regime with 256 draft tokens, JetFlow achieves strong gains, reaching τ=10.7\tau=10.7 and 9.5×9.5\times speedup on MATH-500, and remaining effective on MT-Bench with τ=5.9\tau=5.9 and over 4×4\times speedup. We further integrate JetFlow into industry-grade serving engine and evaluate it across request rates, where it consistently outperforms baselines under small to moderate serving loads, with especially strong gains on higher-end GPUs such as B200. These results highlight the practical potential of JetFlow for reducing decoding latency in serving.

In a nutshell, our work makes the following contributions:

  • •

    We propose JetFlow, a paradigm designed to jointly optimize drafting cost and acceptance rate for speculative decoding. JetFlow trains a causal prediction head with parallel tree-drafting capability, enabling low-cost draft generation while preserving path-conditioned dependencies among draft tokens.

  • •

    We develop and evaluate tree-drafting algorithms that allow speculative decoding to better leverage additional decoding compute. By scaling the draft token budget, JetFlow achieves up to τ=10.7\tau=10.7 and more than 9.5×9.5\times end-to-end speedup.

  • •

    We integrate JetFlow into an industry-grade serving engine and evaluate it under realistic serving scenarios. JetFlow consistently outperforms baselines under small to moderate serving loads, highlighting its practical potential for reducing latency in real-world deployments.

2 JetFlow

2.1 Background

Scaling Bottlenecks in Speculative Decoding.

In speculative decoding (SD), a lightweight approximation model MqM_{q} first proposes NN draft tokens, which are then verified in parallel by the target model MpM_{p} (Leviathan et al., 2023). The target model accepts the longest prefix that is consistent with its own predictions and resumes the next iteration from the first rejected token. The practical throughput of SD depends on both the acceptance rate and the relative drafting cost. Formally, let α\alpha denote the average acceptance rate and let cc denote the cost coefficient between the time for a single step of MqM_{q} and that of MpM_{p}. Under the standard i.i.d. acceptance assumption, the acceptance length per speculative iteration is

𝔼⁡[#​tokens]=1−αN+11−α,\mathbb{E}[\#\mathrm{tokens}]=\frac{1-\alpha^{N+1}}{1-\alpha}, (1)

where NN is the number of draft tokens. Accordingly, the expected walltime improvement over standard autoregressive decoding is

Speedup=1−αN+1(1−α)​(N​c+1).\mathrm{Speedup}=\frac{1-\alpha^{N+1}}{(1-\alpha)(Nc+1)}. (2)

This expression exposes a key scaling bottleneck in speculative decoding: increasing the draft length NN improves throughput only when the acceptance rate α\alpha remains high and the cumulative drafting overhead N​cNc stays small. As NN grows, even modest degradation in α\alpha or non-negligible draft cost can quickly offset the benefit of parallel verification. Figure 2 visualizes that jointly reducing drafting cost and improving acceptance quality is essential for unlocking favorable scaling with longer drafts.

Limitations of Existing Techniques.

Existing work mainly focuses on improving these terms separately. To increase acceptance quality α\alpha, draft-model alignment methods improve agreement between MqM_{q} and MpM_{p} (Zhou et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Goel et al., 2024). Orthogonally, tree-based SD methods such as SpecInfer, Medusa, and EAGLE improve verification efficiency by expanding and verifying multiple candidate branches in parallel (Miao et al., 2024; Cai et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2025).

To reduce drafting cost cc, head-based methods avoid a separately deployed draft model (Cai et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2025). More recently, DFlash pushes drafting overhead to an even lower regime by using block-diffusion-style drafting to generate multiple draft tokens in one draft pass and therefore very low per-token drafting cost (Chen et al., 2026), see Appendix G. However, longer-draft scaling requires both high α\alpha and low cc at the same time, motivating JetFlow that jointly improves drafting efficiency and acceptance quality.

2.2 Head-based Causal Parallel Drafting

Can We Enable Both?

A natural direction to co-optimize both aspects is to combine tree drafting for higher acceptance with parallel drafting for lower cost. However, existing parallel drafting technique like DFlash can break the causal structure needed for effective tree construction: independently predicted future positions are not conditioned on the tokens selected along each branch, leading to inconsistent continuations. JetFlow addresses this challenge by training a causal parallel draft head that preserves branch-wise dependencies while retaining the efficiency of parallel prediction.

Why Causality Matters.

A key requirement for parallel tree drafting is that each node distribution should be conditioned on its own branch prefix. Consider a draft tree rooted at the original prefix xx. Each node vv corresponds to a candidate token yvy_{v}. Let π⁡(v)=(yv1,…,yv)\pi(v)=(y_{v_{1}},\ldots,y_{v}) denote the draft-token path from the root to vv, and let π<v\pi_{<v} denote the ancestor tokens before node vv. Following standard speculative decoding notation, let pp denote the target-model distribution induced by target model MpM_{p}, and let qq denote the draft distribution induced by drafter MqM_{q}. Then q(⋅∣x,π<v)q(\cdot\mid x,\pi_{<v}) denotes the distribution over the candidate token at node vv, conditioned on the concatenated context (x,π<v)(x,\pi_{<v}).

Thus, each node vv at depth ii should be sampled from the continuation-aware distribution q⁡(yv∣x,π<v)q(y_{v}\mid x,\pi_{<v}), rather than from a branch-agnostic per-position distribution ri(⋅∣x)r_{i}(\cdot\mid x) that is not conditioned on the concrete ancestor tokens selected along the branch. Without this causal conditioning, for a candidate branch y1:ky_{1:k}, tree construction ranks branches according to a pseudo-distribution

qsur(y1:k∣x)∝∏i=1kri(yi∣x),q_{\mathrm{sur}}(y_{1:k}\mid x)\propto\prod_{i=1}^{k}r_{i}(y_{i}\mid x), (3)

where rir_{i} denotes the branch-agnostic draft distribution at position ii. Thus, tree construction can favor continuations whose tokens are individually plausible but mutually inconsistent. Verification remains lossless by rejecting invalid prefixes, but the tree itself is optimized under qsurq_{\mathrm{sur}} rather than a causally valid draft distribution, leading to lower acceptance. We provide an empirical case study in Section 3.4.2, with qualitative example in Appendix A.

Architecture.

JetFlow adopts a head-based drafting architecture: the draft head can reuse rich intermediate features from the target model while keeping draft generation cheap. In particular, DFlash shows that a lightweight block-parallel draft head can reuse target-model hidden states and inject fused target-context features into the draft layers’ KV cache for strong target-model guidance (Chen et al., 2026). Building on this design, JetFlow introduces a causal parallel decoding head for tree drafting.

Given a prefix xx, with a corresponding fused hidden state features hxoh_{x}^{o}, the draft head predicts logits for multiple active tree nodes in parallel. Following the standard speculative decoding notation, let MpM_{p} denote the target model and MqM_{q} denote the draft model or draft head, with corresponding distributions pp and qq. The target model defines an autoregressive distribution over a length-kk continuation:

p(y1:k∣x)=∏i=1kp(yi∣x,y<i).p(y_{1:k}\mid x)=\prod_{i=1}^{k}p(y_{i}\mid x,y_{<i}). (4)

To align parallel drafting with this causal factorization, we apply a tree-causal attention mask to the draft head. Each node can attend to the original prefix and its ancestors, but not to descendants or unrelated sibling branches. For two tree nodes uu and vv, the mask is

Mv,u={0,if ​u∈Anc⁡(v)∪{v},−∞,otherwise,M_{v,u}=\begin{cases}0,&\text{if }u\in\mathrm{Anc}(v)\cup\{v\},\\ -\infty,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (5)

where prefix tokens are visible to all tree nodes. The masked attention for node vv is computed as

Attn⁡(Qv,K,V)=softmax⁡(Qv​K⊤d+Mv)​V.\mathrm{Attn}(Q_{v},K,V)=\mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{Q_{v}K^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}}+M_{v}\right)V. (6)

This mask allows all tree nodes to be processed in parallel while ensuring that each branch follows an autoregressive-like dependency structure. More concretely, the tree-causal mask induces a branch-wise draft factorization

q⁡(π⁡(v)∣x)=∏u∈π⁡(v)q⁡(yu∣x,hxo,π<u),q(\pi(v)\mid x)=\prod_{u\in\pi(v)}q(y_{u}\mid x,h_{x}^{o},\pi_{<u}), (7)

This branch-wise factorization mirrors the target model’s autoregressive factorization in Equation 4, but conditions each draft node on the concrete ancestor tokens along its own path. Compared with branch-agnostic block-diffusion drafting in Equation 3, this makes the draft distribution more aligned with the autoregressive MpM_{p} while still allowing logits from all tree depths to be computed in parallel.

2.3 Training

Data Preparation.

We train the draft head on target-aligned sequences, obtained either from the training corpus, as in multi-token prediction (Gloeckle et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2024), or from continuations regenerated by the target model (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2026). Given a sequence (x,y1:k)(x,y_{1:k}), we sample anchor positions and, at each anchor, construct a length-NN training block of NN consecutive future positions. The draft head predicts these NN positions in parallel under a block-causal mask, matching the per-position teacher logits produced by the target model on the same ground-truth prefix.

Distillation Loss.

We train the draft head with a soft-label distillation objective so that the draft distribution preserves the target model’s relative preferences across multiple plausible continuations. Among distillation objectives, forward KL encourages the draft distribution to cover the target model’s probability mass, preserving soft-label information beyond the top prediction. Reverse KL, in contrast, is more mode-seeking and can concentrate probability on high-confidence teacher modes (Gu et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2024). We find this matters in practice (Section 3): reverse KL underperforms substantially, while forward KL slightly outperforms hard-label SFT. We therefore adopt forward KL by default, and present the loss in this form below.

For each active draft position mm, let zq(m)z_{q}^{(m)} and zp(m)z_{p}^{(m)} denote the draft and target logits over the vocabulary 𝒱\mathcal{V}. We define temperature-normalized distributions q~(m)=softmax⁡(zq(m)/TKD)\tilde{q}^{(m)}=\mathrm{softmax}(z_{q}^{(m)}/T_{\mathrm{KD}}) and p~(m)=softmax⁡(zp(m)/TKD)\tilde{p}^{(m)}=\mathrm{softmax}(z_{p}^{(m)}/T_{\mathrm{KD}}), and minimize the forward KL

ℒFKL(m)=DKL​(p~(m)∥q~(m)).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FKL}}^{(m)}=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\tilde{p}^{(m)}\,\middle\|\,\tilde{q}^{(m)}\right). (8)

The final objective is computed over all active draft-token positions induced from the training sequence and normalized by the active-position mask (see Appendix D for details):

ℒtrain=TKD2​∑mwm​ℒFKL(m)∑mwm,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}=T_{\mathrm{KD}}^{2}\frac{\sum_{m}w_{m}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FKL}}^{(m)}}{\sum_{m}w_{m}}, (9)

where mm indexes draft-token positions within sampled blocks, excluding non-loss and anchor-token positions, and TKD>0T_{\mathrm{KD}}>0 is the distillation temperature. This objective preserves the target model’s soft-label preferences and provides teacher-aligned candidate distributions for tree expansion.

2.4 Drafting and Verification

Parallel Tree Drafting.

An overview of the design is shown in Figure 3. At every decoding step ii, the causal draft head conditions on the hidden states hxoh_{x}^{o} of tokens that were verified and accepted in the previous step, and constructs a candidate tree with maximum draft depth NN, branching width WW, and total node budget BB. With one draft-head forward pass, we obtain logits for all draft depths and extract the top-WW candidate tokens at each depth. Tree expansion is then driven by a branch scoring function s⁡(π⁡(v))s(\pi(v)), whose form can vary across implementations; we ablate different choices in Section 3.4. By default, we use accumulated draft log-probability for scoring:

s⁡(π⁡(v))=∑u∈π⁡(v)log⁡q⁡(yu∣x,hxo,π<u),s(\pi(v))=\sum_{u\in\pi(v)}\log q(y_{u}\mid x,h_{x}^{o},\pi_{<u}), (10)

where π<u\pi_{<u} denotes the ancestor tokens before node uu. We then repeatedly pop the highest-scoring expandable node, expand it with up to WW children, and reinsert the children with updated scores until the budget is filled or no expandable node remains. This yields a candidate tree 𝒯⁡(x)={π⁡(v)∣v∈𝒱𝒯}\mathcal{T}(x)=\{\pi(v)\mid v\in\mathcal{V}_{\mathcal{T}}\}, where each path π⁡(v)\pi(v) is a speculative continuation; details are given in Algorithm 1.

Tree Verification.

After constructing the candidate tree 𝒯⁡(x)\mathcal{T}(x), the target model MpM_{p} verifies all tree nodes in parallel using tree attention. For any candidate branch π(v)=y1:k\pi(v)=y_{1:k}, the target distribution factorizes autoregressively in compliance with Equation 4.

The verifier then applies the speculative decoding acceptance rule along each candidate branch. For each draft token yty_{t}, we write the acceptance decision as

At∼Bernoulli(αt),αt=α(yt;q(⋅∣x,y<t),p(⋅∣x,y<t)),A_{t}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\alpha_{t}),\qquad\alpha_{t}=\alpha\!\left(y_{t};\,q(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t}),p(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})\right), (11)

where qq is the draft distribution induced by MqM_{q}, and α⁡(⋅)\alpha(\cdot) denotes the speculative verification rule. In standard non-greedy speculative sampling, this acceptance rule uses rejection sampling:

αt=min⁡(1,p⁡(yt∣x,y<t)q⁡(yt∣x,y<t)),\alpha_{t}=\min\!\left(1,\,\frac{p(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}{q(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}\right), (12)

with a target-model correction token sampled when rejection occurs (Leviathan et al., 2023). The accepted prefix length is a=max{r≤k:At=1,∀t≤r}a=\max\left\{r\leq k:A_{t}=1,\ \forall t\leq r\right\}. In the greedy setting, AtA_{t} becomes deterministic: a draft token is accepted if it matches the target model’s next-token prediction under the same context.

3 Experiments

3.1 Experiment Setup

Models and Datasets.

We evaluate JetFlow on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, covering both dense and MoE target models (Yang et al., 2025). Qwen3 supports both thinking and non-thinking modes, and we use the non-thinking mode throughout our main evaluation for efficient decoding. For training data, we curate 780K examples from the Nemotron Post-Training Dataset V2 (NVIDIA, 2025), including all available coding and math splits, random samples from STEM and chat splits, and 20K additional examples from CodeAlpaca (Chaudhary, 2023). For regenerated training sequences, we apply the corresponding chat template to each data type and continue generation with the target model. We evaluate on math benchmarks including GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MATH-500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021), and AIME25; coding benchmarks including HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), MBPP (Austin et al., 2021), and LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., 2024); and open-ended conversational tasks including MT-Bench (Zheng et al., 2023). All ablation studies are conducted on the math split of Nemotron Post-Training Dataset V2.

Baselines and Training Settings.

We compare against EAGLE-3 and DFlash, two strong head-based speculative decoding baselines (Li et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026). EAGLE-3 uses multi-layer feature fusion for direct token prediction, while DFlash uses a bidirectional block-parallel draft head to generate multiple draft tokens in one pass. DFlash-T constructs draft trees from DFlash’s per-position block-diffusion distributions using best-first tree expansion, resembles DDTree implementation, but uses a pure block-diffusion head trained without loss weighting (Ringel and Romano, 2026). For fair comparison, we train JetFlow and all baselines on the same data mixture using a learning rate of 3×10−43\times 10^{-4} on 8 H100 GPUs. We also ablate DFlash-style loss weighting in Section 3.4; additional training details are provided in Appendix D.

Implementation Details.

For offline inference evaluation, we run experiments on 8 H100 or B200 GPUs. Unless otherwise specified, results in Table 2 use optimized Triton kernels for decoding. For serving-engine evaluation, we integrate JetFlow into vLLM (Appendix E), part of which involve tree verification with a custom SM90 paged FlashAttention kernel using NVIDIA CuTe DSL, extending the paged attention forward path with shared-memory tree-mask staging and tree-tail masking.

3.2 Results

We evaluate JetFlow under both greedy and non-greedy decoding settings in compliance with Equation 12. Evaluation results and comparisons with baselines are summarized in Table 1 and Table 2, and it shows JetFlow consistently outperforms tree-based baselines across all benchmarks.

Low-budget Regime.

Compared with the autoregressive drafting baseline EAGLE-3, JetFlow achieves substantially higher speedup at every reported budget by avoiding EAGLE-3’s higher sequential drafting overhead. At budget 16, DFlash and JetFlow perform nearly the same, suggesting that a short linear draft is already sufficient to cover many high-probability continuations. However, when increasing the budget to 32, JetFlow brings slight improvement, while DFlash often saturates or degrades. This indicates that JetFlow converts the additional draft budget into accepted tokens more effectively.

High-budget Regime.

In Table 2, as the draft budget increases, JetFlow shows a larger gain, e.g. improving from roughly 44–6×6\times to 77–10×10\times speedup on math and coding benchmarks. Whereas DFlash-T scales more modestly to up to 9×9\times, showing causal tree drafting yields higher acceptance than branch-agnostic tree construction. And detailed qualitative example in Appendix A.2 on how causality helps. Under temperature 11, JetFlow remains effective, showing that the benefit of causal tree drafting remains robust under nongreedy decoding.

3.3 System Performance

We evaluate JetFlow in an end-to-end serving setting by integrating tree drafting and verification into vLLM. Serving performance depends not only on accepted length, but also on how the tree budget interacts with batching, verification overhead, memory traffic, and GPU occupancy. Larger budgets can reduce the number of target-model verification rounds, but also introduce higher draft-head and tree-verification cost, making the optimal budget load-dependent.

Budget Allocation.

Table 11 shows that larger tree budgets are most useful at small batch sizes. At batch size 1, increasing the budget from 16 to 256 raises throughput from 443.3443.3 to 968.2968.2 TPS and speedup from 3.09×3.09\times to 6.75×6.75\times. As batch size increases, this gain diminishes: budget 256 drops to 4.51×4.51\times at batch size 16 and 2.85×2.85\times at batch size 32, nearly matching budget 128. This indicates saturation, where the added verification cost and compute pressure reduce the benefit of accepting more tokens per step in throughput improvement.

Practical implication.

These results suggest that tree budgets should be selected according to serving load. Large budgets are preferable in low- to moderate-load regimes, where spare GPU capacity can be used to reduce decoding iterations. Under heavier load, smaller or moderate budgets may be more efficient by reducing per-step overhead and preserving batching efficiency. We evaluate static budget policies in this work and leave dynamic serving-time budget scheduling to future work.

3.4 Ablation Studies

Unless noted, all ablations in this section are evaluated on 4×4{\times}B200 with block size 1616, FlashAttention-2 for the target’s normal forward, Triton tree-attention, and the accumulated draft log-probability heuristic (Equation 10 ) for tree construction at node budget 255255. Reported speedup and average accepted length τ\tau are invariant to hardware under lossless computation.

3.4.1 Training Settings

Learning Rates.

Table 3 reports a grid search over learning rates from 5×10−55\times 10^{-5} to 1×10−31\times 10^{-3}. Very small learning rates underperform and performance plateaus at 3×10−43\times 10^{-4} (peak speedup 8.30×8.30\times), with 6×10−46\times 10^{-4} and 1×10−31\times 10^{-3} within ∼2%{\sim}2\% of the peak.

Loss.

Table 4 compares SFT, forward-KL distillation, and reverse-KL distillation across four math benchmarks. SFT and forward-KL distillation match within ∼3%{\sim}3\% at every dataset, while reverse-KL distillation causes a 3636–46%46\% relative drop in comparison with forward-KL’s, indicating the mode-seeking objective concentrates draft probability mass too aggressively for tree drafting.

Model Generalizability.

Table 5 compares JetFlow and DFlash-T trained on Qwen3-30B-A3B, a MoE target model, with the same 800k data recipe. JetFlow maintains a competitively higher speedups across benchmarks, showing that causal tree drafting generalizes beyond dense Qwen3-8B.

Training Data.

Table 6 studies the effect of using different training data. Regenerated target-model sequences provide the strongest performance, confirming that matching the draft head to the target model’s own generations is important for maximizing accepted length. In contrast, JetFlow -Corpus trains directly on corpus sequences, it underperforms fully regenerated JetFlow , but still achieves consistent speedups across all benchmarks, suggesting that causal parallel drafting can be incorporated during mid-training or even pretraining, where regeneration would be prohibitively expensive.

3.4.2 Tree Drafting with Diffusion Head

Table 7 compares causal and diffusion heads under different choices of γ\gamma, the parameter that controls how aggressively the DFlash training objective downweights per-position loss at positions far from each anchor token. Specifically, position ii within a block contributes to the training loss with weight wi=exp(−max(i−ianchor, 0)/γ)w_{i}=\exp\!\left(-\max(i-i_{\mathrm{anchor}},\,0)/\gamma\right), where γ=0\gamma=0 is interpreted as the limit of uniform per-position weighting (no decay). The causal head is robust across γ\gamma, while the diffusion head is sensitive to γ\gamma and collapses at the endpoints (from 8.36×8.36\times at γ=7\gamma=7 to 5.46×5.46\times at γ=0\gamma=0 and 6.17×6.17\times at γ=15\gamma=15).

A failure example.

On MATH-500 prompt 00 at decode step 00, the diffusion-head draft (γ=0\gamma=0) ranks “ given told that” first in its tree, with cumulative draft surrogate ∑ilog⁡ri=−3.76\sum_{i}\log r_{i}=-3.76 but cumulative target conditional ∑ilog⁡p⁡(yi∣x,π<vi)=−63.32\sum_{i}\log p(y_{i}\mid x,\pi_{<v_{i}})=-63.32 nats: the branch combines two mutually exclusive openers, exemplifying the failure mode of qsurq_{\mathrm{sur}} in Equation 3. The actually-coherent “ are given that the” (target joint −0.08-0.08) sits at rank 3. The causal-head draft on the same prompt ranks “ are told that” first, with surrogate ≈{\approx} target joint (gap −0.34-0.34); tree verification accepts 66 tokens from the causal-head tree but only 44 from the diffusion-head tree (visualized in Figure 4 of Appendix A).

Aggregate generalization.

Across MATH-500 prompts 00–4949, the diffusion-head’s rank-11 gap exceeds the causal-head’s on 92%92\% of prompts, with a median 5×5\times larger (+62.81+62.81 vs. +12.36+12.36 nats); the mean per-step accepted-token ratio is 1.95×1.95\times, closely matching the macroscopic 1.52×1.52\times speedup ratio in Table 7. Full branch-level tables and the rank-11 gap distribution are in Appendix A.

4 Related Work

Speculative Decoding.

Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by drafting tokens and verifying them with the target model (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023). Its speedup depends on draft quality, which controls accepted length, and drafting cost, which controls wall-clock gain. Prior work improves these factors via draft-target alignment (Zhou et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Goel et al., 2024), head-based drafters such as Medusa and EAGLE (Cai et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2025), or draft-free retrieval methods such as Prompt Lookup Decoding, REST, PLD+, SAM Decoding, and SuffixDecoding (Saxena, 2023; He et al., 2024; Somasundaram et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025b; Oliaro et al., 2024). While these methods reduce overhead, they often rely on lexical overlap, retrieval quality, or repeated patterns. In contrast, JetFlow targets low-cost parallel drafting with a learned causal head that preserves branch-wise dependencies for high-acceptance tree verification.

Drafter Alignment.

Previous works train draft models or draft heads to better match the target model. Multi-token prediction objectives supervise future-token predictions during pretraining or midtraining (Gloeckle et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2024), while post-training approaches use supervised fine-tuning, offline distillation, online distillation, or direct acceptance-rate optimization to improve agreement between draft and target distributions (Zhou et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Goel et al., 2024). These methods primarily improve the alignment term that controls acceptance rate. JetFlow is complementary: it trains the drafter not only to match the target model, but also to preserve the causal structure needed for budgeted tree construction, so each branch is expanded from continuation-aware draft distributions.

Parallel Decoding and Drafting.

Parallel decoding methods reduce latency by relaxing strict one-token-at-a-time generation. Self-speculative decoding drafts with early target-model layers and verifies with later layers (Elhoushi et al., 2024). Diffusion LLMs refine multiple tokens per iteration (Wu et al., 2025; Qian et al., 2026). Jacobi-style methods preserve causality by parallel fixed-point updates, with recent consistency distillation works improving convergence to autoregressive outputs (Fu et al., 2024; Kou et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2025a). These methods increase tokens committed per forward, but are typically applied to the target model itself. DFlash is the closest baseline, generating multiple draft tokens in one block-parallel pass (Chen et al., 2026); however, its branch-agnostic block-diffusion predictions are not explicitly optimized for causal tree construction.

5 Conclusion

We presented JetFlow, a causal parallel tree drafting framework for speculative decoding that jointly addresses the two factors limiting end-to-end speedup: drafting latency and accepted length. By preserving branch-wise causal dependencies while generating candidate trees in a single low-cost draft-head pass, JetFlow makes tree construction better aligned with the target model’s autoregressive factorization. Across dense and MoE Qwen3 models and vLLM serving settings, JetFlow consistently turns larger draft budgets into higher wall-clock speedup, for MATH-500, reaching 9.64×9.64\times on Qwen3-8B, 9.45×9.45\times on Qwen3-30B-A3B, and over 6×6\times serving speedup on a single H100 under low-to-moderate load. These results show that block-level causality conditioning over prefix hidden states is key to scaling speculative decoding with parallel drafting that is both cheap and effective.
